headline: Every formal check on Alpöge's proof has now finished and passed. The last one, lake comparator v4.36, reported "Your solution is okay!" at 21:49 UTC on Nov 25, after 122 hours. Masullo's revised draft hasn't appeared yet.

proofs.name: Alpöge + Claude
proofs.claims: RH and GRH for Dirichlet L-functions
proofs.form: 4-page note + Lean 4 archive: 175,187 modules, about 17 million lines, no paper

stages.note: Every check has finished and passed. Compiles, 3 standard axioms only, accepted by nanoda, con-leche, lean4lean, Lean's default kernel and Lean's paranoid kernel; statement matched by comparator, con-leche and con-ron. A sandboxed rebuild on a separate machine gave a byte-identical export. Unmodified Comparator v4.33.0 passed Nov 23. Nov 25: lake comparator v4.36 on the canonical challenge passed end to end, its paranoid, nanoda and default kernel stages all accepting, "Your solution is okay!".

No full human-readable proof exists. Alpöge says a prose version would run past 250,000 pages. Digests have started: Rubinstein's 164-page working guide to the zeta case reduces RH to one inequality over primes, and takes that inequality from the Lean code without proving it. Several other reconstructions are in progress.
Certified by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative. Not by Clay, which still lists RH as unsolved.

proofs.name: Masullo
proofs.who: Alessandro Masullo (Stanford PhD under Brian Conrad), all human
proofs.form: 940-page draft, "The Music of the Primes", 12 years of work, not formalized

stages.note: Posted by Ravi Vakil Nov 20, released early
Not in Lean. Vakil asked people to formalize it.

Conrad has read it for months; says it is undergoing major revision. Reported problems now have specifics: a theorem that fails a test at the prime 2, and a bound claimed for Markushevich bases that is only known for Schauder bases. Chapter 13, where GRH should be deduced, holds only placeholders. Masullo's own site says the Nov 20 draft was never meant to be public in this state, with revisions due in the coming months. No revised version yet.
Vakil now makes no claim the strategy is correct

timeline.text: Starts working with Claude across several areas of math, per the timeline in his note (which he says Claude assembled).
Masullo and Conrad spend four and a half hours at a blackboard with Peter Sarnak at the IAS.
Last entry in Alpöge's timeline: GRH.
Alpöge posts Remark, a 4-page note, with the Lean archive in 14 parts. Claims RH and GRH, formalized without extra assumptions.
Terence Tao blogs it alongside two Alpöge Euler/Navier-Stokes blowup results, and points to the Lean Zulip as the place to follow verification.
All 175,187 modules compile (Lean 4.33.1). #print axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.
leanchecker replays every module through the Lean kernel: 175,187 of 175,187, zero rejections.
nanoda, an independent kernel written in Rust, accepts the full 61 GB export in 27 min 42 s on 80 threads.
Ravi Vakil, AMS president, posts a hurried announcement: Masullo has a proposed all-human proof of GRH, which Conrad has been reading closely for months.
Scientific American: independent mathematicians say the AI proof is almost certainly true; Buzzard says a comparator run is still awaited.
con-leche accepts the full export in verified mode (3 min 15 s, 64 threads), and its compare mode finds all five headline theorems justified against the independent challenge.
lean4lean passes all 175,187 compiled modules. Five decide +kernel computations needed a raised step limit.
Simon DeDeo finishes a second full kernel replay from his own build: 175,187 of 175,187 accepted, 3 h 22 min.
About 8 hours later Vakil updates: several people reported problems in Masullo's proof, found with help from AI models. He makes no claim the strategy is correct.
Clay president Martin Bridson calls it an announcement of historic significance, and says it is a very long way to any award. Clay still lists RH as unsolved.

The proof combined with Robin1984, an independent formalization of Robin's and Lagarias's criteria, gives two divisor-sum inequalities that never mention zeta. con-leche and nanoda accept the combined export.
Robin1984 itself passes unmodified Comparator v4.33.0 and lake comparator v4.36 from exports: Lean paranoid, nanoda and Lean default kernels all accept.
Status page: every finished check passes. lake comparator (Lean 4.36) and the Lean default + paranoid kernels on the export are still running.
Main proof's lake comparator has passed statement comparison and the axiom check; its kernel stages and the Lean default + paranoid replay are still running, single-threaded.
Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative: full confidence the proof is correct; they certify both statement and proof.

A fresh lake build inside a sandbox with no network, on a separate machine, ends with zero errors, and the export made inside it is byte-identical to the published 61 GB one. One of 175,187 compiled files differs, traced to a known Lean race over a bound-variable name, which kernels ignore.

Michael Rubinstein (Waterloo) reports his own run from Alpöge's archive: full compile, standard axioms only, a kernel replay of all 175,187 modules, and nanoda on the 1,484,729 declarations the theorems use, all with no errors. He also posts a 164-page working guide to the zeta case, which takes its key inequality from the Lean code without proving it.
con-ron, the Rust port of con-leche, accepts the export in verified mode, and its compare mode finds all five theorems justified against the challenge.
Status page: lake comparator's kernel stages and the Lean default + paranoid replay still have no verdict.

John Baez posts a simplified sketch of Masullo's strategy (zeros as an operator's spectrum, primes as closed orbits in a trace formula) and two reported problems: a theorem that predicts log 2 on a test function near 2 where a review computes 0, and a boundedness claim on page 444 that holds for Schauder bases but apparently not Markushevich bases. He notes Chapter 13 has placeholders where the GRH deduction should be.
Status page: still no verdict from lake comparator's kernel stages or the Lean default + paranoid replay, single-threaded and running since Nov 20.

Vakil says this is probably his final update. He has not yet looked at the draft himself and calls it outside his expertise; maths questions go to Conrad, and he points to Baez and Lozano-Robledo for updates.

Masullo opens his own site. It keeps the Nov 20 draft untouched for the record, says it was never meant to be seen publicly in this state with revisions due in the coming months, and posts a summary of the statements.
Lean's paranoid kernel, run with one allocator setting changed, accepts the full export after 10 hours on one thread (peak memory 98.8 GiB). The same check with default settings is still running.

Unmodified Comparator v4.33.0 finishes end to end after 64 hours: statement comparison and axiom check pass, nanoda and Lean's default kernel accept, and it reports 'Your solution is okay!'. Still running: lake comparator v4.36 and the default-settings paranoid replay.
Lean's paranoid kernel with default settings (leanchecker-paranoid, Lean v4.36.0) accepts the full export after 72 h 20 min on one thread.

Main proof's lake comparator v4.36: its paranoid kernel stage accepted at about 19:53 UTC and its nanoda stage at about 21:31 UTC. Its last stage, Lean's default kernel, started then and runs single-threaded; run on its own, that check took 48 hours and accepted.

lake comparator v4.36 finishes on the canonical challenge after 122 h 45 min: statement and axiom checks pass, Lean's paranoid kernel, nanoda and Lean's default kernel all accept, and it reports 'Your solution is okay!'. Every check has now finished.

voices.name: Andrew Sutherland
voices.said: Ran most of the public checks. Says the chance anything is fishy is about zero.

voices.name: Kevin Buzzard
voices.said: The first question is whether the Lean statement is the real theorem. Wants a successful comparator run, ideally in paranoid mode across several kernels.

voices.name: Lean and Mathlib communities
voices.role: joint statement, endorsed by the Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative
voices.said: Full confidence the proof is correct. The statement is Mathlib's, two tools matched it, and several kernels, including formally verified ones, accept the proof; all four of Buzzard's criteria are met.

voices.name: Terence Tao
voices.said: Calls Alpöge's an enormous Lean-only proof; has only read declaration statements. Says Masullo's draft will take time to digest and partly goes down an F_1 route like Connes'.

voices.name: Elliot Glazer
voices.said: Says the formalized statement in the drop is in fact GRH.

voices.name: Michael Rubinstein
voices.said: Repeated the main Lean checks himself with no errors, and is writing a classical-style guide to the zeta case. Calls it a work in progress that still leans on the Lean code for its central inequality.

voices.name: Brian Conrad
voices.said: Says the paper is undergoing major revision and needs a more final stage before the method can be judged. Posting now was the less bad of two bad options.

voices.name: Ravi Vakil
voices.said: First: so far looking good. Then: problems reported, every issue must be resolved, no claim of correctness. Now: probably his last word, he has not read the draft, and questions go to Conrad.

voices.name: Alessandro Masullo
voices.said: Says the Nov 20 draft was never meant to be seen by the public as it stands. It stays up unchanged for the record, with revisions due in the coming months.

voices.name: John Baez
voices.said: Stresses he is no number theorist and his sketch is tentative. Thinks the reported objections could prove fixable or mistaken, and points out the draft's final chapter is still placeholders.

voices.name: Alex Kontorovich
voices.said: Describes an out-of-body feeling at hearing himself say RH has been solved.

voices.name: Martin Bridson
voices.said: Historic significance; a long, difficult road to real understanding and a very long way to any award.

voices.name: Association for Human Mathematics
voices.said: Objects that nobody understands or can answer for the proof, and that this way of producing results puts technical validity ahead of understanding. Urges mathematicians to keep their research independent of AI companies.

seal_read.one_line: Alpöge's RH is proved in the formal sense, and every check, the official comparator included, has now passed. Masullo's probably isn't, as written.

odds.label: Alpöge's Lean proof is a valid proof of RH as mathematicians mean it
Masullo's draft survives as a proof of GRH (fixable gaps allowed)

why: Three kernels written by different people, in different languages, accepted the same 61 GB proof term. For the proof to be wrong, all three would need the same soundness bug, or the statement would need to be wrong.

The statement is Mathlib's own RiemannHypothesis, which predates the drop, and con-leche matched all five theorems against a challenge written independently. Sutherland also plugged the proof into a separate formalization of Robin's criterion and got a statement about divisor sums that never mentions zeta. That makes a subtly wrong zeta definition a much smaller risk.

The first build ran unsandboxed, which left room to wonder what the checked export really was. A rebuild from a fresh download, with no network and a read-only source tree, gave the same export byte for byte. That closes it, but it was never where I put much of the doubt, so the number stays.

The Lean and Mathlib communities, with the Lean FRO behind them, now certify statement and proof. That's the people who'd know best putting their names on it, though it adds judgement, not a new check.
Rubinstein's run at Waterloo is one more machine and one more person getting the same answer. It uses the same kernels as the earlier checks, so it doesn't move the number either.

Nov 23 moved me from 97 to 98: Lean's own kernel and its paranoid kernel both accepted the full export, and an unmodified Comparator run passed end to end. That is most of what Buzzard asked for. The paranoid kernel then accepted with default settings too, which removes the tuned-setting caveat but adds no new kernel, so the number stays.

Nov 25: lake comparator v4.36, the official judge run on the canonical challenge, passed end to end, with Lean's paranoid kernel, nanoda and Lean's default kernel all accepting. That's the last of what Buzzard asked for. It doesn't move the number much, since each of those kernels had already accepted the export on its own, but the formal check is now finished.

The 2% left no longer sits in whether a kernel accepts it. It's whether the formal statement and the Mathlib definitions under it, riemannZeta and the challenge file, really say RH, plus five decide +kernel steps that needed raised limits, and the human review nobody has done yet.

Masullo: a 940-page draft its own advisor calls under major revision, whose last chapter, the one that should deduce GRH, is still placeholders. Two concrete problems are now public, at the prime 2 and in a functional-analysis step, on an F_1-style route in the spirit of Connes and Deninger that has never been closed. His own site now says the draft wasn't meant to be read yet. Conrad's months of reading is why it's 8% and not 1%.

What nobody has yet, for Alpöge's: understanding. The first human-readable guides are appearing, but the furthest along still takes its central inequality from the Lean code on trust. A proof no human can read settles a fact about the zeros. It isn't yet mathematics anyone owns.
change_mind: Someone shows the challenge statement, or a Mathlib definition it rests on like riemannZeta, doesn't quite say RH.
A Lean kernel soundness bug that the proof's decide +kernel steps actually use, shared by every kernel that accepted it.
A human reconstruction hits a step that's false in ordinary mathematics.
For Masullo: Conrad says publicly the gaps are closed, or a reported problem is shown to be fatal.

explainer: The Riemann zeta function is ζ(s) = 1 + 1/2^s + 1/3^s + ..., extended to every complex number s except s = 1.
It is zero at -2, -4, -6, ... (the trivial zeros) and at infinitely many other points, all known to lie in the strip where the real part of s is between 0 and 1.
RH says every one of those other zeros has real part exactly 1/2. It was stated in 1859 and has been checked for the first 10 trillion zeros.
If true, the number of primes up to x differs from the integral of 1/log t by at most about √x·log x. GRH says the same for Dirichlet L-functions, which control primes in arithmetic progressions.
